1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4.background: The 1886 World Championship match between Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort introduced the first modern ideas: Steinitz gave the pawn back and left White with an isolated d4-pawn. Alexander Alekhine added new ideas, and the line was played at the highest level from the 1930s. It declined after the Second World War as the Indian Defences gained ground, but several elite players returned to it in the late 1990s, and it is currently considered sound.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3.strategy: The classical main line: develops a piece, guards d4 and takes the e5 square away, so Black cannot strike at the centre with the e-pawn. White regains the pawn at leisure with the bishop and keeps a flexible, comfortable game against Black's counterplay.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Saduleto Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4.background: An old move that became popular again in the 1990s.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4.strategy: Builds the broadest possible centre at once and frees the c1-bishop to develop. The c4-pawn can be recovered later, because Black has no central pawn and must strike at White's pawns quickly or be squeezed. The most ambitious way to answer the pawn grab.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3.background: Strong players have often employed it, among them Anatoly Karpov.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3.strategy: A quiet way to regain the pawn: it guards d4 and opens the f1-bishop, which takes back on c4 by development rather than by a pawn move. The price is that Black gets time to strike at the centre, and the typical result is an isolated d-pawn for White.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Qa4+.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Accelerated Mannheim Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Qa4+.strategy: Checks and prepares to win the c4-pawn back with the queen. It works, but the queen stands exposed on the edge of the board, where Black gains time with natural developing moves. Black equalises easily, and White has nothing in the centre to show for the early queen sortie.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5.strategy: Strikes back at once, before White's knight can come to f3 to guard d4. Grabbing the pawn with dxe5 backfires, since ...Qxd1+ forces the queens off and costs White castling. Black gets open piece play, and White will probably end up with an isolated d-pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight fights for the centre and watches e4, leaving White to retake the pawn with the bishop. Black accepts that gain of time for sound development and keeps ways to challenge White's centre later.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e6.strategy: The classical, conservative answer: Black accepts that White will win the pawn back and builds a solid pawn structure instead of striking at the centre. The cost is the c8-bishop, shut in behind the e6-pawn, and a slightly easier game for White than after the more active replies.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4.strategy: Regains the pawn with a developing move and points the bishop at f7. Taking on e5 instead loses the right to castle after the queen trade, so White lets Black capture on d4 and chooses afterwards between a calm recapture, giving an isolated d-pawn, and a sharper try.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and guards d4, but does not win the pawn back at once. Black can gain space with ...e4, driving the knight away, or take on d4 and reach the main line by another route. White gets an ordinary game, but a less direct one than recapturing on c4.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and prevents ...b5, which would drop a pawn to Nxb5, but leaves the c4-pawn for later. Black can exchange on d4 and use the open e-file and the pin ...Bb4 to gain time, so White has to be sure the lead in development is real.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 exd4.strategy: Takes the central pawn and attacks e3 in the same move, so White has to decide at once how to deal with the pawn on d4. Black has won White's d-pawn for now and keeps the initiative in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece towards the centre but leaves the tension on d4 and e5 unresolved, so White decides how it is settled. Sound, yet Black gives up the clear target in the centre that capturing on d4 creates.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 Bb4+.strategy: Develops with check, so White must block. Black can then trade off the dark-squared bishop and ease the game. The check wins no real time, and the bishop leaves home early for a modest exchange.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 exd4 5..strategy: Instead of recapturing, White aims queen and bishop at b7 and f7 together, hoping to catch Black's king in the centre. It is a gambit: with accurate defence White is a pawn down and has to prove the pressure is worth it.

Recaptures with the pawn: White accepts an isolated d-pawn in return for open lines for the pieces and quick development, while the bishop on c4 already eyes f7. Black must show the isolated pawn can be attacked. The standard, healthiest way to continue.

Takes back the pawn with the queen, which Black can challenge at once with ...Nc6 and so trade queens. White keeps its castling rights and a sound structure, but a queenless game gives it little to play for beyond equality.

Parries the double attack: the queen guards f7, while the c8-bishop already guards b7. From e7 it also eyes the e3-pawn that the d4-pawn attacks, and the b4-square for a check. Black keeps the extra pawn and White must justify the gambit.

Guards f7 from f6 and supports the d4-pawn, so Black keeps the extra pawn. The queen blocks the g8-knight's natural square and does not pin the e3-pawn as ...Qe7 does, so White can recapture on d4 at will. Playable, but a step behind the main defence.

Guards f7 along the seventh rank, while the bishop keeps b7 covered. The queen, though, blocks the c8-bishop's route and the knight's natural square, and White may still recapture on d4. Safe enough, but passive.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 exd4 5..name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation, Christensen Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 exd4 5..strategy: The most natural way to carry on the gambit: the knight develops, attacks the d4-pawn and prepares castling, so White's pieces work together against Black's king. Black is a pawn up and has to untangle the c8-bishop and secure the king.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 exd4 5..name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation, Novikov Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 exd4 5..strategy: Blocks the e1-a5 diagonal against ...Qb4+, but the knight can be pinned there and shuts in the c1-bishop. After ...dxe3 the bishop cannot recapture, and fxe3 opens the f-file in front of the king, so Black keeps the extra pawn comfortably.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 exd4 5..name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation, Billinger Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 exd4 5..strategy: Takes b4 from the black queen, so ...Qb4+ no longer gains a tempo, and keeps the threat of exd4. Sound but slow: a rook-pawn move develops nothing, and Black uses the time to bring out a knight.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 exd4 5..name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation, Korchnoi Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5 4.Bxc4 exd4 5..strategy: Steps off the e-file and the e1-a5 diagonal, so ...dxe3 and ...Qb4 gain no tempo, at the cost of castling. The king on f1 boxes in the h1-rook until White spends time untangling it: playable, but awkward.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4.strategy: Takes back the c4-pawn with the bishop, which lands on its best diagonal, while the centre stays intact. Black has no central pawn to disturb it, so White emerges with comfortable development and a small, lasting space advantage.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight before recapturing, reaching the mainstream set-up of the opening by another move order. White still wins the pawn back, but gives Black the chance to pin the knight with ...Bg4 before the bishop recaptures on c4.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight before recapturing, but Black cannot hold the pawn: ...b5 drops a pawn to Nxb5, and the bishop retakes on c4 next move. White only gives Black a free move to strike in the centre, so this is a less exact order than recapturing at once.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6.strategy: Opens the way for the f8-bishop and prepares to strike at d4 with the c-pawn. Solid, but the pawn on e6 shuts in the c8-bishop, which has to be rerouted to the long diagonal or settle for a modest square.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 at once, before White's knight can support it. If White takes on c5, Black can trade queens, which costs White the right to castle; if White develops, Black can still follow with the solid ...e6. A flexible, respected way to undermine the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 a6.strategy: Takes b5 from the bishop and prepares ...b5 to chase it with a gain of time. It spends a move before the centre has been challenged, so White gets a free hand to develop. Sound, but slower than striking at d4 at once.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.strategy: Brings out the last piece needed before castling and guards d4, which will be Black's target. Nothing sharp: both sides finish development, and the game turns on whether Black can undermine White's centre.

Develops the queen's knight where it supports a later advance of the e-pawn and watches d5. A natural, flexible move, though it commits the knight before Black has shown how it will challenge d4, and the bishop on c4 can still be chased by queenside pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.Q.strategy: Prepares an advance of the e-pawn with the queen behind it and keeps the bishop on c4 covered. The queen takes a square White's own development needs, though: ...Bb4+ forces White to block with a piece, so development is a little awkward.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Classical Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.strategy: The central break the whole set-up prepares: Black hits d4 at once, hoping to remove White's centre pawn or saddle White with an isolated one. Black gave back the extra pawn for exactly this freeing move, and it is the main line.

Develops the bishop and prepares to castle, keeping every plan open while White finishes development. Black strikes at the centre a move later than in the sharper set-ups, so White gets a moment to build a broad centre first.

A useful preparatory move: it readies ...b5 to chase the bishop from c4 and gain queenside space. Black commits only to this plan and keeps the choice of central break for later, which suits a flexible, patient game.

Develops the queen's knight to its natural square and prepares a central advance with the e-pawn. It accepts that the bishop will be chased, but the advance of the b-pawn also loosens Black's queenside, so the position stays balanced.

Castles and completes the kingside development, keeping every plan open. Black's ...a6 has committed to queenside space, so White does not need to prevent ...b5 and can simply retreat the bishop, playing for the centre while the king is safe.

Takes the bishop out of the reach of ...b5 and keeps it on the diagonal aimed at e6 and the black king's side. White spends a move on the retreat, but Black's ...a6 has then gained little, and ...b5 can be met by a4.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Normal Variation, .. a6 Sideline
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.strategy: Attacks the bishop at once and gains queenside space with a tempo. The price is a loosened queenside: the b-pawn can no longer guard c6, so that square becomes weaker.

Challenges the centre at once and keeps the threat of ...b5 against the bishop in reserve. White must decide whether to resolve the tension or to castle, and Black gets the standard counterplay against d4 with a useful move already made.

A solid developing move that gets the king ready to castle. It spends the move on development rather than on the break against d4, so White gets time for a central advance with the e-pawn, and Black must be ready to meet it.

Gets the king to safety before the centre opens; with the knight and bishop already placed, castling completes the kingside development and brings the rook into play. White does not need to hurry and can wait for Black to show its plan.

Prepares to push the e-pawn with the queen behind it and keeps the bishop on c4 covered. It delays castling, so it is a slightly slower route than playing O-O at once, but it keeps White's options open.

Develops the queen's knight and prepares a central advance with the e-pawn, but puts the knight where ...a6 and ...b5 gain time against the bishop. White gets a normal game, with less than castling at once offers.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Normal Variation, Traditional System
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.strategy: Takes b5 from the bishop and prepares ...b5 to drive it back with a gain of time. It is the main-line idea of the opening: Black gains queenside space and a good square for the c8-bishop at the price of a slightly loosened queenside.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Normal Variation, Traditional System
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.strategy: Completes kingside development and secures the king in the same way. Both sides are now safe, and the game turns on the centre: Black looks for a pawn break against d4, while White's space gives it the more comfortable game if the break is delayed.

Strikes at d4 at once instead of preparing ...b5. If White takes on c5 and the queens come off, Black regains the pawn in a level, quiet game; if White keeps the tension, ...a6 and ...b5 are still available.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Classical Defence, Normal Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.strategy: The main line: the king is safe and the rook can come to the centre before the tension is resolved. White waits for Black to commit and keeps the choice of how to meet the pressure on d4, whether by taking, advancing or supporting.

Supports a later advance of the e-pawn and lets White take on c5 without allowing the queens off. The queen also covers the bishop on c4 against queenside pawn pushes, at the price of delaying castling and leaving the king in the centre.

Releases the tension and invites an early queen trade. Black can take the queens off at once, which costs White the right to castle, and regains the pawn on c5 with ...Bxc5. The exchange leads to a level, rather drawish game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Classical Defence, Main Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.background: The traditional continuation after 3.Nf3, reached in thousands of games.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.strategy: The classical main line: it prepares ...b5 to drive the bishop from c4 and win queenside space, while the tension on d4 stays. White has to decide at once how to meet the threat of ...b5, and Black gets a flexible, balanced game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Classical Defence, Steinitz Variation, Development Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.strategy: Develops a piece with a second attack on d4, so the tension is real at once. Black accepts slower queenside play, without ...a6, in exchange for quick development and a firm grip on the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Classical Defence, Steinitz Variation, Exchange Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.background: Named after Wilhelm Steinitz and well known since his 1886 match with Zukertort, it is rarely seen in modern practice.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bxc4 e6 5.N.strategy: Resolves the tension at once and leaves White with an isolated d-pawn after the recapture. The early clarification gives White's pieces a free hand, and Black's play against the pawn is slow. Playable, but White's active pieces make it the less comfortable choice for Black.

Prepares ...b5 to hit the bishop with a gain of time, and takes b5 away from it. The queen on e2 stands ready to support a central advance, but Black has enough counterplay and the position is balanced.

Adds a piece to the pressure on d4 and develops the queen's knight, keeping ...a6 and ...b5 in reserve. Black does not yet challenge the bishop on c4, so White gets a move to settle the centre, but the position stays balanced.

Settles the central tension with a trade that leaves White an isolated d-pawn. White's pieces gain open lines in return, and the queen on e2 already bears on the e-file, so Black must prove the pawn is a weakness. Playable, but it gives White the more active game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 e5.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Central Variation, McDonnell Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 e5.background: The first known game with it was played in 1834 between Alexander McDonnell and Louis de La Bourdonnais. It is the main reply to 3.e4.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 e5.strategy: The main reply: Black opposes the pawn centre at once and opens the f8-bishop. White has to be exact, since grabbing on e5 or c4 at once goes wrong, and the game becomes open and highly theoretical, with Black fighting for equality in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 Nf6.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Central Variation, Alekhine System
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 Nf6.strategy: Hits the e4-pawn at once and invites White to push it, since a pawn on e5 can become a target. Black lets White have space and plays against the centre with active pieces, but has to prove the advanced pawns are overextended.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 Nc6.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Central Variation, Modern Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 Nc6.strategy: Pressures d4 with a piece, using the fact that White has no knight on f3 yet to defend it. Black fights for the centre with pieces instead of pawns, in a modern, active set-up that keeps White from building freely.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Central Variation, Rubinstein Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5.strategy: Undermines the base of White's centre with a pawn. If White advances, the position gets a pawn structure where White has space in the centre and Black plays on the queenside, with the pawn on c4 still to be won back.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 b5.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Central Variation, Greco Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 b5.background: Rarely seen, though its popularity rose in the 2020s after the discovery of 6...Qb6; 3...e5 remains more popular.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 b5.strategy: Tries to keep the extra pawn by supporting it. Risky: White attacks the base of the pawn chain, the queenside is loosened, and White's lead in development gives more than enough compensation for the pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 f5.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Schwartz Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 f5.strategy: Hits the e4-pawn, but weakens the king's diagonal: Qh5+ is check at once, and exf5 takes the f-pawn and opens the position while Black is undeveloped. Black has the extra pawn on c4, but the king pays for it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.d5.strategy: Gains space and closes the centre, taking away the d5-square and cramping Black's pieces while the c4-pawn is still to be won back. White gets a lasting space advantage, so Black must create queenside counterplay.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.dxc5.strategy: Takes the pawn and invites a queen trade that costs White the right to castle. Black wins the c5-pawn back while White still has to win back its own pawn on c4, so the exchange leaves the position level and gains White nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and guards d4, but does not decide the centre. Black can exchange on d4 and remove the pawn that would give White space, while the c4-pawn is still to be won back. A sensible but unambitious choice that gives up the space grab of the main line.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.d5 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on the e4-pawn and keeps the pawn on c4 for now. The natural, flexible reply: Black plays against White's advanced pawns with pieces and aims for queenside counterplay.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.d5 b5.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Central Variation, Rubinstein Defence, Yefimov Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.d5 b5.strategy: Tries to keep the extra pawn, but nothing defends the b5-pawn: White's a-pawn attacks it at once, and once it falls the c4-pawn loses its only support. Black loses the gambit pawn and more, while White keeps the space gained with d5.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.d5 e6.strategy: Challenges the d5-pawn at once. If it is exchanged, the e-file opens in front of White's uncastled king and Black's pieces gain room, though White's centre and lead in development keep chances for the initiative. The c8-bishop stays hemmed in until the structure clears.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.d5 Nf6 5.Nc3.strategy: Defends the e4-pawn with a developing move and keeps the space advantage that d5 gained. White intends to win the c4-pawn back by development, leaving Black cramped and short of room for the pieces.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.d5 Nf6 5.Qa4.strategy: Checks to win the c4-pawn back at once, since the queen covers e4 from c4 as well. The queen comes out early and Black develops with the check parried, so White regains the pawn but gains little more. Sound, but slower than defending the centre by development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.d5 Nf6 5.Nd2.strategy: Defends the e4-pawn and attacks the c4-pawn together, but blocks the c1-bishop. Black can try to keep the pawn with ...b5, so White's recovery is not guaranteed, and the position stays sharper than after the main reply.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.d5 Nf6 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Linares Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5 4.d5 Nf6 5.Nc3.strategy: Keeps hold of the c4-pawn and bids for queenside space, but the b-pawn is undefended: the knight on c3 can take it at once. Black has to show that the active knight and the loosened position give enough play. Sharp and double-edged.

The thematic break: Black challenges the d5-pawn now that White has committed the knight, and after ...exd5 the e-file opens against a king that has not castled. White keeps a small plus, but Black's pieces get open lines and active play.

Attacks the queen, but White just plays f3 and the bishop has to go back, so Black has spent two moves to end up where it started. White gains time and space, and e5 then drives the f6-knight away, while the c4-pawn still needs defending.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 e5 4.Bxc4.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Central Variation, McDonnell Defence, Somov Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 e5 4.Bxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn back at once but leaves d4 loose: ...Qxd4 trades queens and Black gets a stable centre, so White has to work to win the d4-pawn back. Sound and roughly level, but Black chooses the simplification.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 e5 4.Nf3.strategy: The principled move: it attacks the unprotected e5-pawn and guards d4 in the same move, so Black has to settle the centre at once. White then regains the gambit pawn with comfortable development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 e5 4.dxe5.strategy: Takes the e-pawn and lets Black trade queens: ...Qxd1+ forces the king to recapture, so White loses the right to castle. Material is level and the position playable, but White's king stands in the centre while Black develops with ease.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 e5 4.d5.strategy: Cramps Black with a space-gaining pawn but overextends: White has not yet regained the c4-pawn, and Black undermines the centre with ...c6 or ...Bb4+ while keeping the extra pawn.
